t.7.85.1: When the night had given way to dawn, the two, having bathed and made offerings into the sacred fire, sang here and there just as the sage had instructed them before.
t.7.85.2: Kākutstha heard, part by part, that account of deeds of old, an unprecedented form of recitation richly adorned with song.
t.7.85.3: Having heard from the two boys the song, composed in many metres and accompanied by the rhythm of the lute, Rāghava became filled with curiosity.
t.7.85.4: Then, during an interval in the rites, the king, a tiger among men, having assembled the great sages and the kings, as well as the learned men and the townsfolk,
t.7.85.5: Having gathered together all of them, the experts in the ancient lore, those learned in words, and the aged twice-born, he had the two singers take their seats before them.
t.7.85.6: There the delighted hosts of sages and the mighty kings, as if drinking with their eyes, gazed upon the king and upon those two singers.
t.7.85.7: Then all of them spoke to one another in unison: "Both resemble Rāma, like an image drawn forth from an image."
t.7.85.8: If they did not have matted locks, if they were not wearing garments of bark, we would find no difference between the one singing and Rāghava.
t.7.85.9: While they were conversing thus, the two sons of the sage there began a song that heightened the joy of the listeners.
t.7.85.10: Then began a sweet, superhuman music of the Gandharvas, and none of the listeners could reach satiety with that wealth of song.
t.7.85.11: Beginning from the very start, the two sang the cantos that open with the sight of Nārada, and from there onward they sang the cantos up to the twentieth.
t.7.85.12: Then, in the afternoon, having listened to those twenty cantos, Rāghava, who was devoted to his brothers, spoke to Bharata.
t.7.85.13: Give quickly, O Kākutstha, eighteen thousand pieces of gold to these two great-souled boys; let not their labor be in vain.
t.7.85.14: Kuśa and Lava did not accept that gold as it was being given to them, and the two great-souled ones, astonished, said, "What use is this to us?"
t.7.85.15: We two are forest-dwellers, content with the wild fruits and roots of the forest. What shall we do with gold and riches here in the forest?
t.7.85.16: As the two of them spoke thus, the listeners, filled with curiosity, and Rāma as well, every single one, were utterly astonished.
t.7.85.17: And Rāma of great splendour, eager to hear about the origin of that poem, questioned those two, both of them sons of a sage.
t.7.85.19: To Rāghava, who was questioning them, the two sons of the sage spoke these words: "The blessed Vālmīki is the author, who has come near to the sacrifice, and by whom this entire story has been revealed to you."
t.7.85.18: What is the extent of this poem, and what is the standing of the great-souled one? And who is that bull among sages, the author of this great poem?
t.7.85.20: From the very beginning, O lord of kings, there are five hundred cantos. As far as your life and its foundation extend, so far, O king, are the auspicious and the inauspicious recounted.
t.7.85.21: If, O king, great chariot-warrior, you have set your mind on hearing it, then, finding a moment of leisure between your tasks, listen to it together with your younger brothers.
t.7.85.23: Rāma too, having heard the sweetness of that song, went to the hall of the sacrificial rite together with the sages and the great-souled kings.
t.7.85.22: Rāma said, "So be it," and the two of them, having taken leave of Rāghava, went joyfully to the dwelling where that bull among sages was staying.
